definition: Assail means to attack vigorously with blows or words.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word assail. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know assail should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The moment tickets went on sale, angry season-holders assailed the box office with calls, emails, and one hand-delivered spreadsheet.
To question a plan is the gentlest challenge there is, far short of assailing it.
Criticize finds faults one at a time; it stops short of assail, which batters the target from every side at once.

Attack is the plain, general word for going after a target — a single punch or one harsh review is an attack. Assail multiplies it: the blows or criticisms come in waves, from every side, without letup. You can attack once; to assail is to keep the attacks coming.

To bombard is to overwhelm with a continuous stream — questions, emails, artillery — and the word cares only about volume. Assail adds intent to damage: an assailed target is under hostile attack, not merely flooded. Fans bombard a star with friendly requests; hostile critics assail her performance.

To lambaste is to thrash someone in words alone — one scathing review or furious editorial can lambaste. Assail is broader and bigger: it covers verbal and physical sieges alike, and its signature is attack arriving from every side. One critic lambastes a film; a whole chorus of critics assails it.

The word's picture is physical: a leap at the target.
Assail turns criticism into a siege — use it when attacks come in volleys, physical or verbal.
Its unit-mates divide the labor: berate targets a person to their face at length, rail vents loudly against something, and assail presses an attack meant to damage.
